newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Spain-led group buys Brazil's Coelba.
newsitem.headline: Spain-led group buys Brazil's Coelba.

text.p: A consortium led by Spain's Iberdrola bought a controlling stake of Brazilian power distributor Coelba for 1.73 billion reais, 77.3 percent above the base price, officials said.

An official at the Rio de Janeiro bolsa said the group, which includes Brazil's largest pension fund Previ and Banco do Brasil's brokerage arm BB DTVM, beat out bids by four other groups for the 65.64 percent stake of Coelba voting capital.
The winning bid was well above market expectations of a 30 to 40 percent premium.
Coelba, owned by the Brazilian state of Bahia, is the third Brazilian power firm to be privatized and Iberdrola's bid was the largest premium yet offered in the privatization of a local power firm.
Light, which was owned by the federal government, and Rio de Janeiro state's Cerj were sold last year.
Brazil's National Development Bank (BNDES) has offered to finance up to 50 percent of the 975.8 million real minimum price set for Coelba.
Bahia state, in Brazil's impoverished Northeast, plans to offer an additional 5.5 percent voting stake to Coelba employees.
Iberdrola was member of a consortium that clinched the bids earlier this month on two Rio de Janeiro state gas firms -- Cia Estadual de Gas (CEG) and Riogas.

At Thursday's Coelba auction, the Iberdrola-led group easily beat out offers led by Chilean-owned Cerj, private Espirito Santo state power firm Escelsa, French-owned Light, and U.S.-based Central and Southwest Services Inc.
The nearest bid was from the Escelsa-led consortium, which offered 1.62 billion reais. All the groups included foreign partners.

Analysts said Coelba had taken a number of steps ahead of the privatization to improve efficiency and boost its financial results, including cutting staff by 1,500 to 4,700 employees over the last three years and reducing its debt to healthier levels.
They said the company also is in a good position to invest in power generation in the future and serve as a springboard for future power privatizations in northeastern Brazil.
((-- Simona de Logu, Rio de Janeiro newsroom 5511 2485413))
